title: Control Plane ↔ Runtime Interop Migration Chronicle
content:
Purpose
This is a working chronicle for migrating private deployments to the new control-plane API (v2) while upgrading runtime nodes to runtime-2.x images. Focus is on preserving client API compatibility, minimal disruption for customer-managed VPC/on-prem installs, and providing a clear rollback story. This doc captures an end-to-end plan, pragmatic Terraform notes, cutover sequences, validation checks, and unresolved questions.

Scope & Non-Goals
- Scope: coordinated upgrades where control plane (CP) and serving runtime (SR) are versioned separately. Includes DB migrations (meta/state), KV cache compatibility, and API-contract shims.
- Non-goals: full re-architecture of control plane; cluster-level tooling changes unrelated to CP/SR compatibility.

High-level constraints
- Many customers run air-gapped or VPC-isolated clusters with strict upgrade windows (2–4 hours).
- Some older clients pin to API v1 or rely on behavior quirks (tokenization, streaming frames).
- Terraform modules must not force re-creation of large resources during control plane rollout.

Compatibility index (quick view)
- CP v1 <-> SR 1.x: baseline, no migration needed.
- CP v2.0: introduces schema v2 for routes and rollout policies, but includes runtime-facing compatibility headers (X-RW-Compat: 1->2).
- SR 2.x: supports both KV-format v1 and v2, reads v1 keys and writes v2 when flag enable_kv_migration=true.
- Shim behavior: CP v2 will accept legacy client requests if legacy-header present; we recommend feature-flagged shims at ingress.

Pre-upgrade checklist (customer-facing prerequisites)
1) Config backup: export control-plane-db snapshot + runtime-state tarball.
2) Terraform plan: produce plan with exact diffs; dry-run in staging clone.
3) Add compatibility feature flags: cp.accept_legacy=true, runtime.enable_kv_migration=false initially.
4) Confirm support-window and rollback window with customer ops.
5) Coordinate network egress for image pull if on-prem.

Terraform module notes (practical tips)
- Keep modules additive. Avoid renaming resources that would destroy stateful instances (e.g., redwood_control_plane -> control_plane_main).
- Introduce new submodule control_plane_v2 and route it behind conditional var.use_cp_v2. This lets us create v2 alongside v1 for canary traffic.
- Example var usage: var.cp_version = "v2"; resource control_plane[cp_version] { lifecycle { prevent_destroy = true } }
- Important: for DB migration resources, use aws_db_snapshot (or equivalent) with copy_tags = true to preserve metadata.
- When updating IAM/policies, stage the new role and attach to a non-critical instance before switching traffic, to avoid permission flips that cause 500s.

Cutover strategy options (pick one per customer)
A) Shadow Canary: deploy CPv2 alongside CPv1. Route 1–5% of traffic to CPv2. Observe for 24–48h, increase if stable.
B) Rolling CP Upgrade: replace control-plane nodes one-by-one, relying on in-place backwards-compatibility shims. Good when DB schema has online migrations.
C) Blue/Green (preferred for major schema changes): provision a full CPv2 environment, run migration in isolated DB copy, smoke test, then switch DNS/load-balancer and rotate runtimes with minimal TTL.

Recommended sequence (blue/green variant)
- Step 0: Preflight checks (see validation list below).
- Step 1: Provision CPv2 cluster + supporting infra using new Terraform module with a new prefix to avoid resource name collisions.
- Step 2: Restore DB snapshot to a staging DB, run migration tool in dry-run mode, validate migration artifacts.
- Step 3: Boot a subset of SR nodes with SR 2.x in the staging environment, enable runtime.enable_kv_migration=false. Run integration tests against CPv2.
- Step 4: Run traffic-shaping experiment: mirror production traffic to staging CPv2 (no write-through). Validate request/response parity for 72h.
- Step 5: If parity is acceptable, schedule a live cutover window and notify customer.
- Step 6: During cutover, flip LB to CPv2 then progressively update SR nodes to SR 2.x and enable runtime.enable_kv_migration=true on a per-node basis.

Rollback plan (concise)
- Immediate rollback: switch LB/DNS back to CPv1 and stop SR 2.x instances (replace with SR 1.x images).
- DB rollback: if DB schema migration was destructive, have a pre-cutover snapshot to restore. Practice full DB restore in staging before live.
- Rolling rollback: drain and recreate nodes with previous images; Terraform life-cycle prevent_destroy protects critical infra.

Validation & smoke tests (run in sequence)
1) Health probes: GET /health, /internal/kv-status returns expected key counts.
2) Token-level scenario: generate tokens for a small user, assert identical completions from CPv1 vs CPv2 for mirrored requests.
3) Streaming parity: compare chunked frame timings and headers (X-RW-Stream-Version). Tolerances: 200ms median delta.
4) Latency SLO checks: p50/p95 must not regress > 20% for a 1-hour mirror test.
5) Cold-start cap: measure model load times for typical 2-4k context sizes.

Observability checklist (must-haves before cutover)
- Tracing: distributed headers enabled and trace sampling at 10% for initial canary.
- Logging: structured logs include fields: cp_version, runtime_version, request_id, migration_flag.
- Metrics: expose compatibility_mismatch_count and kv_migration_conflicts.
- Alerts: set a short-duration alert for error-rate > 1% post-cutover in first 2 hours.

Known gotchas & notes from earlier experiments
- KV key namespace collisions: enabling write-through when not all SR nodes are migrated can lead to mixed key namespaces. Mitigation: use per-node migration token and gradual write migration.
- Client SDKs that rely on subtle response-ordering may break under new stream framing; maintain shim until SDKs are updated.
- Terraform drift: state moves when modules reorder resources. Run state-show on critical resources and confirm IDs before apply.

Unresolved questions / action items
- Q: Should we change default streaming frame size in CPv2? Action: perf run with top-10 customers and summarize. Assignee: Liam.
- Q: Can we safely compact v1 KV keys after 30 days? Action: create eviction policy RFC and run customer opt-in.

Appendix: quick commands & test snippets
- Check pods (k8s on-prem): kubectl get pods -n redwood --selector=app=control-plane -o wide
- Compare responses (small python snippet): curl -H "X-RW-Mirror: true" https://cpv2.example.com/generate | jq .text > v2.txt; curl https://cpv1.example.com/generate | jq .text > v1.txt; diff v1.txt v2.txt
- Terraform plan verification: terraform plan -var="cp_version=v2" -out=plan.out && terraform show -json plan.out | jq '.["resource_changes"] | length'

Notes to readers
- This is a working chronicle — many sections are intentionally practical and include TODOs. If you are executing a live migration, follow the Checklist exactly and ping #private-deployments at the start and end of the window.
- If customer is strictly air-gapped, add manual steps for image delivery and hashed manifests into the preflight section.

Revision history
- 2025-11-12: initial draft (Priya)
- 2025-12-05: added Terraform lifecycle patterns and blue/green sequencing (Xiaowen)
- 2026-01-10: appended parity test thresholds and action items (Liam)

TODOs
- Add a runbook template for DB restore with exact commands per DB engine (Postgres, MySQL).
- Create a lightweight migration simulator repo that mirrors 1% production traffic and validates CP/SR parity.

End of chronicle.
